title: Forming a memory
subtitle: An experience becomes something retrievable
question: What happens when you remember something new?
teaser: Look around a room you have never seen, then watch it turn into a memory.
intro: Storing a memory is not recording. An experience arrives spread across a dozen different systems, and something has to tie those pieces into one thing you can pull back up later. That tying-together is picky, it favours whatever mattered at the time, and it keeps getting revised long afterwards.

events.title: The experience arrives in pieces
events.explanation: Objects, layout, sounds, how the room felt — all handled by different systems, none of which knows about the others.

events.title: Content is identified
events.explanation: Things get recognised and sorted. What goes into memory is this interpreted version, not what actually hit your eyes.

events.title: Where things are
events.explanation: Where things are gets handled separately from what they are. 'Where' and 'what' arrive at memory by different routes.

events.title: Through the gateway
events.explanation: Everything funnels into one doorway — the way in and out of the memory system.

events.title: Binding
events.explanation: The pieces get tied into a single thing you can retrieve as a whole. That is what makes it an episode rather than a list of facts.
events.science: Hippocampal damage impairs forming new memories for events while leaving skill learning and immediate conversation largely intact — the clearest evidence that memory is not one system.

events.title: Context is bound in too
events.explanation: When and where become part of the memory too. It is why a smell can drop you back into a specific room.

events.title: Not everything is kept equally
events.explanation: Not everything is kept equally. How much something mattered decides how strongly it sticks — and that gets decided before you have a say.
events.science: Arousal at the time of an event is associated with better retention of its central details. What felt important is what survives.

events.title: Attention gates encoding
events.explanation: Whatever you did not pay attention to often did not get stored well enough to find again. Divided attention costs you the memory.

events.title: Reactivation
events.explanation: Over the following hours and nights, the same patterns get replayed in bursts, with nothing happening to trigger them.
events.science: Coordinated hippocampal–cortical reactivation during rest and sleep is well documented, and interfering with it impairs later retention.

events.title: The cortex is recruited
events.explanation: That replay reaches the parts that originally did the seeing and hearing, strengthening the links between them.

events.title: The representation changes character
events.explanation: Over time, finding the memory depends less on the hippocampus and more on connections spread across the brain. Nothing was copied or moved — what changed is what retrieval leans on.
events.science: This is systems consolidation. The strong version — that memories eventually become fully hippocampus-independent — is debated, especially for vivid, detailed episodic recall.

events.title: And it keeps changing
events.explanation: And it keeps changing. Detail drops away, the gist stays, and every time you retrieve it you can alter it.
events.science: Retrieval is itself an encoding event. Remembering can strengthen, distort or update the memory being retrieved.

causalChain.label: Experience arrives distributed
causalChain.detail: The experience arrives in pieces, handled by systems that do not know about each other.

causalChain.label: Content is interpreted
causalChain.detail: What gets stored is your interpretation, not the raw input.

causalChain.label: Convergence at the gateway
causalChain.detail: Everything funnels through one doorway into the memory system.

causalChain.label: Binding
causalChain.detail: The pieces get tied into one retrievable thing.

causalChain.label: Selection by relevance
causalChain.detail: What mattered and what you attended to decide what survives.

causalChain.label: Reactivation
causalChain.detail: Replay during rest and sleep makes it more stable.

causalChain.label: Reliance shifts
causalChain.detail: Finding it comes to depend on a different, more spread-out set of connections.

science.text: Damage to the hippocampus and surrounding structures impairs the formation of new memories for events while sparing many other kinds of learning.
Attention at the time of an experience strongly predicts whether it can later be retrieved.
Coordinated reactivation of recent activity patterns occurs during rest and sleep, and disrupting it impairs retention.
Retrieving a memory can change it. Memory is reconstructive rather than reproductive.
We show encoding as a single binding event. It is continuous, overlapping, and distributed across the whole experience.
The 'Now / 1 day / 1 week / 1 year' control compresses processes that unfold over very different timescales into one visual axis.

Nothing here is a memory moving from one place to another. The brightening cortical network represents a change in what retrieval depends on — not a file transfer. We are deliberately avoiding that metaphor.
How completely a memory can become independent of the hippocampus is an open question, and the answer appears to differ for gist and for vivid detail.

references.label: Medial temporal lobe amnesia
references.note: Case and lesion work establishing the role of hippocampal structures in forming new episodic memories.

references.label: Systems consolidation
references.note: The proposal that memory representations gradually change their dependence on hippocampal versus cortical structures over time.

references.label: Replay during sleep
references.note: Findings that patterns active during experience are reactivated in coordinated bursts during subsequent rest and sleep.

references.label: Reconsolidation
references.note: Work showing that retrieved memories can enter a labile state and be modified.

readouts.label: Encoding strength
readouts.note: How strongly the model ties this experience together.

readouts.label: Detail retained
readouts.note: How much specific detail survives, as opposed to just the gist.

readouts.label: Modelled durability
readouts.note: How well it holds up over the days that follow.

outcome.headline: Encoding
outcome.body: An experience that arrived in pieces across a dozen systems got tied into something you can pull back as a whole. Then it was selectively strengthened, replayed while you were not using it, and gradually came to depend on a different set of connections.
outcome.insight: You did not choose what to remember. The choice was made during the experience, using what mattered and what you were attending to — and it is still being revised.
